en: Magma rising through the Earth's crust causes Taal Volcano to erupt and release ash into the air.
Warm Pacific Ocean water evaporates and rises to fuel the strong winds and heavy rain of Philippine typhoons.
Deep underground magma heats groundwater in Tiwi to produce steam that spins turbines and generates renewable electricity.
Warm, shallow, sunlit waters allow coral polyps in Tubbataha Reef to extract calcium and build massive limestone structures.
Heavy rainfall in the Sierra Madre mountains causes rapid water runoff that quickly overflows the banks of the Cagayan River.
Weathered volcanic ash from Mayon Volcano releases essential minerals into the soil, helping Bicol's abaca plants grow stronger fibers.
The moon's gravitational pull attracts the water of Manila Bay, causing the daily rising and falling of ocean tides.
Moist winds from the Pacific Ocean hit the Sierra Madre mountains, forcing the air upward to produce heavy rain on the eastern slopes.
The sudden collision and sliding of the Philippine Sea Plate against the Eurasian Plate releases energy that shakes the ground in Luzon.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the limestone bedrock in Palawan to carve out the massive chambers of the Puerto Princesa Underground River.
The steep slopes of the Cordillera mountains cause fast water runoff, which the carved Ifugao rice terraces slow down to prevent soil erosion.
The temperature difference between the Asian landmass and the Pacific Ocean creates pressure changes that drive the seasonal Amihan and Habagat winds.
